text.body:
An Introductory Comment
This final pair of sermons presents a unique case in the Wesley corpus. What we have here is one sermon on the same text, in two versions (one in English, the other in Latin). They are so nearly alike that one is tempted to suppose that we are dealing with an instance of translation. They are, however, different enough to suggest a single project in two different drafts. What little we know of the actual circumstances supports this latter conjecture.
As one of the twelve Fellows of Lincoln College, Wesley had been expected to proceed to the degree of Bachelor of Divinity within seven years after his Master of Arts degree (1727). The reasons for his failure to do this are not clear. At any rate, in 1736, while he was in Georgia, he was elected to the only fellowship in the college (the so-called ‘canonist fellowship’) exempted from the B.D. requirement. Moreover, he continued to hold this fellowship, at considerable inconvenience to the college, until his resignation in 1751.
That Wesley remained mindful of the expectations of his college, even after his forsaking it for his new role in the Revival, can be seen in an aside in a letter written from Bristol, October 27, 1739, to his brother Samuel in Tiverton. His main interest in this letter is a sprightly defence of his new career against his brother’s sharp criticisms of it. But he also adds the following bit of ‘news’:
In a few days, my [younger] brother and I are to go to Oxford to do exercise for our [B.D.] degrees. Then, if God enables me, I will prove my charge [of works-righteousness] against Bishop [George] Bull, either in my Latin sermon, or Supposition Speech.
No mention is made of this in the Journal, but it is recorded there that John and Charles turned up in Oxford on November 12. However, three days later, the belated news of their brother’s sudden death (November 5) came to them, and they immediately set out for Tiverton.
JWJ, November 20-24, 1739. For a time, with the excitements and demands of the burgeoning Revival, the matter of an academic degree drops out of John’s sight. And yet, despite his absence from Oxford and his mounting public notice, the
university officials were still prepared to invite him to take his regular turn as preacher to the university—this time on July 25, 1741 (i.e., during ‘Long Vacation’, when the majority of the dons and students would be absent). He seems to have regarded such an invitation as a twofold opportunity: to deal with his own academic arrears respecting that deferred B.D., and also to deliver a long-considered diatribe against the university as a whole, on the charge of its manifold lapses in doctrine and discipline. The Journal entry for June 18 confirms this:
I inquired concerning the exercises previous to the degree of Bachelor of Divinity; and advised with Mr. Gambold concerning the subject of my sermon before the university; but he seemed to think it of no moment. ‘For’, said he, ‘all here are so prejudiced that they will mind nothing you say.’ I know that. However, I am to deliver my own soul, whether they will hear or whether they will forebear.
Incidentally, though, this exchange with Gambold, with other things, seems to have led to a rupture, for the Journal entry for July 2 reports matter-of-factly: ‘I met Mr. Gambold again, who honestly told me he was ashamed of my company.’
On this visit to Oxford, he had returned again to his ‘charge against Bishop Bull’
JWJ, June 24, 1741. by re-reading the latter’s Harmonia Apostolica—ignoring Robert Nelson’s careful explanation that Bull’s doctrine of justification was not Pelagian.
Nelson, The Life of Dr. George Bull (1714), pp. 95-99. And, even earlier (June 19, according to the diary), Wesley had ‘writ plan of sermon’ on the same day that he had ‘read the Canons of the Council of Trent’. It was, therefore, a time of theological reading and reflection, as if in ‘cramming’ for an examination.
Wesley’s diary indicates that he was also writing three Latin exercises (geneses), on predestination, on the means of grace, and on justification, presumably to satisfy the lecture requirement for the degree (JWJ, June 20, 1741); see G. R. M. Ward, Oxford University Statutes (Oxford, 1848), I:55. Cf. JW MS ‘S. Paulus per totum 7m ad Rom. caput…’ (number ‘3’ at the top), in MA. On the 22nd, there is a note that he had written out a ‘plan of Latin sermon’ (i.e., one of the B.D. exercises).
The Statutes (Tit. VI.6.2) required that a person standing for admission to the degree of Bachelor of Divinity ‘preach in his own person, and not by deputy, a Latin sermon in the church of St. Mary the Virgin’. Ward, Statutes, I:55. These scattered bits of evidence allow for the conjecture that he was preparing a sermon for St. Mary’s in which he could ‘deliver his soul’ and also satisfy one of the B.D. requirements.
As far as we know, nothing came of this plan. Apparently, Wesley was dissuaded from preaching the sermon on Isa. 1:21 in St. Mary’s (and by Lady Huntingdon, no less). And there is no record of his ever having
submitted anything officially for that B.D. degree. Instead, for the university sermon on July 25 he wrote out a different piece, on a text he had tried before, on Acts 26:28 (see No. 2, The Almost Christian). And when he returned to St. Mary’s for the last time in 1744 (see No. 4, Scriptural Christianity), he couched his denunciation of the university in very different terms.
It is all the more remarkable, therefore, that Wesley took the necessary pains to preserve both the English and Latin holographs of these two unpreached sermons. The manuscript in English that is transcribed here exists in nineteen numbered duodecimo pages now in the Colman Miscellany in the Methodist Archives, Manchester. After Wesley’s death, it passed into John Pawson’s possession and was published in 1797 in the Arminian Magazine
XX.265-69, 317-22. with a misleading foreword by Adam Clarke:
The following sermon was found in a mutilated manuscript among Mr. Wesley’s papers. It is dated June 24, 1741. A Latin copy of the same discourse has also been discovered. Mr. Pawson, with great care, copied the former, and I have supplied the deficiencies out of the latter. On collating both sermons, I find several variations, and though not of any great importance, yet sufficient, in my judgment, to vindicate the propriety of translating and publishing the Latin one, not merely as a matter of curiosity, but of utility. The sermon, no doubt, was written with the design of being preached before the University of Oxford, but whether it ever were preached there, cannot be determined.
The English text was then reproduced by Joseph Benson in his edition of the Works,
(1812), XI.72-85. with minor alterations and one major addition in I.7 (three paragraphs added from the Latin). Benson also supplied it with its triumphalist title, ‘True Christianity Defended’. Thomas Jackson followed Benson faithfully in both title and text.
The holograph of the Latin sermon, dated by Wesley June 27, 1741 (three days after the English version), has also survived; it is in the Morley Collection in Wesley College, Bristol. It is the most extensive example we have of Wesley’s prowess with neo-Ciceronian Latin—an impressive reminder of his grounding in the classics at Charterhouse and Christ Church. The English version here follows Wesley’s own holograph. The Latin version is presented here for the first time: its orthography has been modernized, with Wesley’s abbreviations fitted out (e.g., the enclitic -que which he regularly shortens to -q at the endings of conjunctive nouns), and a few obvious lapses have been corrected silently. It is placed here in sequence to the English text, with its [04:392]own annotation, so that either version may be read separately and yet also compared with the other. For the English text, a few notes are offered (besides the usual annotations) calling attention to significant omissions, or variations between it and its Latin counterpart. In the transcription of the latter, and in the notes on various peculiarities of Wesley’s vocabulary and syntax, I have had the generous help of an expert Latinist, Fr. Placid Gilbert, O.S.B. (Cist.), of the Abbey of Our Lady of Dallas (Texas).
Hypocrisy in Oxford [Latin text] Isaiah 1:21 Quomodo civitas fidelis meretrix facta est!
The MS orig. had no text and no title; Adam Clarke later added the Scripture citation and the Latin quotation to the first page, along with a wrongly transcribed date from the last page: ‘Jan. [June] 27, 1741’.
It was natural enough that Wesley would not have used any particular Latin text of the Bible; he appears to have translated freely into Latin. Similarities to other standard texts are noted (Vulgate, Theodore Beza, Johannes Tremellius).
1. Quum adducturus sum contra terram aliquam gladium, inquit Dominus Iehovah, si speculator videns gladium supervenientem terrae, clanxerit buccina et monuerit populum—tum quisquis audit sonum buccinae, et non acceperit monitum, si adveniens gladius sustulerit ipsum, sanguis eius in ipsius capite erit. Ipse vero speculator, cum viderit gladium advenientem, si non clanxerit buccina, populusque non fuerit monitus, et adveniens gladius sustulerit ex eis aliquem: hic propter iniquitatem suam tolletur, sanguinem vero eius e manu speculatoris reposcam.
[Cf.] Ezek. 33, ver. 2, etc. [Tremellius].
2. Dubium non est, quin et istum lehovae verbum ad quemvis evangelii praedicatorem pertineat, ‘Te autem, O fili hominis, te inquam, speculatorem dedi domui Israelis: ut audiens ex ore meo verbum, moneas eos ex me. Quum dixero improbo, improbe, omnino moriturus est, si non loquaris monendo improbum, ut desistat a via sua: ipse improbus propter iniquitatem suam morietur, sanguinem vero eius e manu tua requiram.’
Ver. 7, 8 [Tremellius].
3. Neque speculator iste, inimicus ideo nobis censendus est, quod vera nobis loquatur: quippe quem ad id impellit, non magis timor Domini, quam infucatus
An unusual usage: the negative of fucatus (‘painted, dyed’); hence infucatus would mean ‘not dyed’ (i.e., ‘genuine’ or ‘sincere’). proximi amor. Alioquin, hanc [04:409]minime ingrederetur viam, qui eiusdem exitum probe novit. Meminit enim sermonis quem dixit Christus, ‘Me mundus odit, quoniam ego testor de eo, opera eius mala esse.’
John 7:7 [Beza]. Et, ‘Non est servus maior domino suo.’
Chap. 15:20 [Vulgate and Beza].
4. Mihi tamen manet alta mente repostum, me vobis. Fratres, hoc saltem amoris pignus, et Almae Matri, a qua plusquam viginti annorum spatio tot tantaque beneficia accepi, hoc grati animi indicium prorsus debere, ut ex ore Domini vos aperte moneam; ut implens ministerium quod ab ipso accepi quae pernecessaria sunt vera loquar. Vellem sane, quemlibet alium, mihi vobis forsan minus accepto, provinciam hanc praeripuisse. Siluerint omnes, mox clamabunt lapides, ‘Quomodo civitas fidelis meretrix facta est!’
5. Quam fidelis olim fuerit Domino suo, civitas haec nostra in monte constituta, cui ut illibata Virgo desponsata fuerat, testentur inclyti ipsius filii; quos nulla dies unquam memori eximet aevo, donec omnia consummentur. Quo amore sponsum illum filiis hominum pulchriorem, semper fuerit prosecuta, qua observantia, omnia ab eo praescripta exceperit, quam presse vestigiis ipsius inhaeserit; testetur martyrum quos enutrivit sanguis, in aure Domini Sabaoth altius insonans, quam ‘si linguae centum oraque centum’. At iam quantum mutatur ab illa! Quomodo meretrix facta est, peregrinorum voci auscultans!
See John 10:5. Iam derelicto Domino suo, semet ipsam corrumpi passa est.
I. Quoad doctrinam,
II. Quoad mores.
I. Et primo, quidem loco, quoad doctrinam.
1. Dici sane non potest, incorruptam Christi doctrinam a nobis penitus exulare: absit ut dicam, omnes illos autores, quos gremio suo fovit academia, vel quorum scripta plurimorum apud nos manibus teruntur, a recto tramite aberrantes perversa loqui, et non secundum evangelium quod accepimus. Sunt, qui viva Dei oracula explicuerunt, eodem spiritu quo sunt scripta. Sunt qui solidum illud, cum Ecclesia nostra, fundamentum posuere, in quod portae inferni non praevalebunt.
Matt. 16:18 (Vulgate and Tremellius). Sunt etiam (benedictus sit [04:410]Pater luminum, omnis donationis bonae et integrae Dator)
See Jas. 1:17 (Beza). qui superaedificarunt super fundamentum hoc, non ligna, faenum, stipulam, verum aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, quales dies iste nunquam perituros declarabit.
See 1 Cor. 3:12-13 (Beza).
2. Gratias eo quoque nomine Deo agamus oportet, quod etiamnum oculis conspiciamus, et audi[a]mus
Taking both conspiciamus and audiamus as subjunctives. ipsi, qui verum pacis evangelium,
See Rom. 10:15. et veritatem annuntiant quae est in Jesu.
See Eph. 4:21. Sed quam pauci! Et ex altera parte, quam multi, οἱ καπηλεύοντες
2 Cor. 2:17; see No. 36, ‘The Law Established through Faith, II’, I.1 and n. sermonem Dei! Quantum cibi salubrioris animae invenimus! In quantam veneni vim impingimur! Quam raros aut legimus aut audimus genuinum Christi evangelium praedicantes, [et] purum illud inquam et simplex evangelium quod eximiis Sacrae Scripturae fontibus desumptum, veneranda mater nostra Ecclesia Anglicana, in Articulis, Homiliisque suis nobis ob oculos posuit? Quum nos undique circumvallent, qui neque Ecclesiae nostrae doctrinas, neque S[acras] S[criptura]s, neque Dei potentiam comperientes, multas sibimet inventione[s] extuderent,
I.e., ‘to beat out’; it also has a pejorative import: ‘to extort’, ‘to squeeze out’; see Eccl. 7:29; cf. Lewis and Short, A Latin Dictionary. unde et alios indies a simplicitate Christi corrumpunt?
3. Non intelligi velim de istis πρωτότοκοι τον Σατανᾶ
See ‘The Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians’, VII.1, in The Apostolic Fathers (Loeb, 24:292). quocunque venient nomine, qui Dominum cuius sanguine redempti sunt abnegantes, celerem sibi ipsis, perniciem accessunt. Famosi isti paulum damni nobis valent inferre. Quid vero, si qui Ecclesiae nostrae columnae visi, si acerrimi qui dicuntur fidei propugnatores, ipsam vere Ecclesiam prodiderunt, fideique quam ab ipsa edocti sumus, fundamenta prorsus evellerunt?
4. Ut ingratum opus hoc quam citissime absolvam unum et alterum tantum scriptorem adducam, eos vero multa et pietatis et eruditionis laude cumulatos; qui ipsum Ecclesiae nostrae fundamentum evellere sunt conati, dum primariam nostrae, quin et omnium ecclesiarum quae Reformatae audiunt, doctrinam, nempe iustificationem per fidem solam, strenue oppugnarunt!
5. Horum alter, plures scripsit et antequam vita functus est, in
publicum protulit conciones, eo fine ut probatum daret, non fidem solam, verum et omnigena bona opera necessario requiri, priusquam quis possit iustificari. Supervacuum plane foret, aliqua ex iis verba citare, quum omnia aperte in eundem scopum collineent: quem quidem abunde praemonstrat ipse titulus concionum, qui est, ‘Necessitas Regenerationis (quam omnem Sanctitudinem vult complecti) in Ordine ad Iustificationem.’
Tillotson, Vol. 1, Conc. LI, etc. [Tillotson’s Sermons were never published in Latin; this is a back translation of Wesley’s.]
6. Mirum forsan aliquibus videatur, reperiri ex angelis ecclesiae Dei,
See Rev. 2:1, etc. eumque tam in nostra, quam in exteris gentibus, existimatione hominum vix cuiquam secundum, qui incaute adeo fundamentalem ecclesiae cui praefuit doctrinam lacessiverit. Quis vero non ex imo suspiret corde quum ex eadem parte stantem viderit, praesulem aliis titulis omni laude maiorem; et quum a tanto viro haec ipsissima verba audierit.
‘Dicitur homo ἐξ ἔργων δικαιοῦται (ex operibus iustificari)
Jas. 2:24 (Beza). quia bona opera conditio sunt, iuxta ordinationem divinam in evangelico foedere stabilitam necessario in hoc requisita ut quis iustificetur, hoc est remissionem peccatorum per Christum partam obtineat.’
Bulli Harm. Apost., p. 4 [I.8, slightly abridged and altered].
Paulo post, testimonia in hanc propositionem probandam adducturus, inquit, ‘Prima classis erit eorum quae generatim de bonis operibus loquuntur, tanquam conditione necessaria requisita ut quis iustificatur.’ Sequuntur loca quaedam Scripturae. Deinde adiicit, ‘Quis non videt hisce in locis quasi cumulum bonorum operum, quae si quis non praestiterit, ei spes veniae ac remissionis peccatorum omnino intercluditur.’
Ibid., p. 8 [II.3, abridged and altered].
Interiectis quibusdam, addit, ‘Praeter fidem, etiam resipiscentiam ad iustificationem necessario requiri nemo est qui non videat. Porro, resipiscentia non est opus unicum vel simplex, sed multorum aliorum operum quasi complexio[nem]. Suo enim ambitu comprehendit sequentia opera: (1) de peccatum tristitiam; (2) humiliationem sub manu Dei; (3) peccatorum odium; (4) peccatorum confessionem; (5) ardentem misericordiae divinae implorationem; (6) amorem Dei; (7) a peccatis [04:412]cessationem; (8) firmum novae obedientiae propositum; (9) male partorum restitutionem; (10) remissionem peccatorum quae in nos proximi peccarunt; (11) opera beneficentiae, sive eleemosynas. Quae quanti valeant ad remissionem peccatorum a Deo impetrandam, satis liquet ex Daniele c. 4º. com. 27º: ubi regi Nebuchadnezzari adhuc in peccatis haerenti, salubre hoc consilium suggerit propheta, peccata tua eleemosynis redime, et iniquitates tuas misericordiis pauperum.’
Ibid., p. 10 [II.6-7, abridged].
7. Quae si ita sint, actum est de fundamentali Ecclesiae Anglicanae pariter ac omnium reformatorum doctrina, nempe iustificationem per fidem solam. Abiiciendi sunt Religionis Articuli; abiiciendus uterque Homiliarum liber; utpote eidem prorsus fundamento innixi. Verum res ad examen non iam revocanda est. Impraesentiarum pro concesso sumitur, Ecclesiam vera docere: a qua tamen isti scriptores et innumera paene tum scriptorum tum praedicatorum turba, ab iis edocta, immane quantum discrepant!
This section, not in the English version, may be translated as follows: ‘But if this is the case, then the fundamental doctrine of the Church of England and of all Reformed churches as well—viz., justification by faith alone—is discarded. Moreover, the Articles of Religion are abandoned and, by the same token, the books of the Homilies, since they are based on the very same foundation. What is worse, the issue is not even left open for further consideration. Nowadays, it is generally assumed that the church teaches the truth; and yet here are these authors, together with a multitude of other writers and preachers educated by them, deviating from the truth by a wide margin.’
8. Verum enimvero supponamum fundamentum rite locatum, ita ut iam moveri nequeat, nedum evelli. Quisque videat tamen quomodo superaedificet. Respicite vos ipsos, ne perdamus quae egimus, sed ut mercedem plenam recipiamus.
These opening sentences, not in the English text, may be translated: ‘But surely I can assume that the foundation has been laid so soundly that it cannot really be moved now, much less torn up. Even so, it behooves everyone to take care how he builds upon this foundation. Look well to yourselves, therefore, that we may not lose what we have been given, but that we may receive our full reward.’ Cf. 1 Cor. 3:10-14. Quem in finem sanctimoniae eiius saepissime meminit Ecclesia, sine qua nemo Dominum videbit.
See Heb. 12:14 (Vulgate and Beza). Eam vero in precatione illa singulis ad minus septimanis repetita optime describit, ‘Purifica cogitationes cordium nostrorum per inspirationem Spiritus Sancti, ut te perfecte amemus, et sanctum nomen tuum debita veneratione celebremus.’
BCP, Communion, Collect for Purity. Postrema haec verba, ‘Sanctum nomen tuum
debita veneratione celebremus’, totam sanctimoniam seu religionem externam complecti satis manifestum est: Sicut, et ista, ‘Purifica cogitationes cordium nostrorum,’ negativam internae partem exprimere, cuius altitudo et profunditas, est cor purum, ex inspiratione Spiritus Sancti. Quae restant verba, nempe, ‘ut perfecte te amemus’, positivam (quod aiunt) sanctimoniae partem continent. Quum amor ille totius legis sit adimpletio,
See Rom. 13:10. imo mens ipsa quae fuit in Christo.
See Phil 2:5.
9. Iam vero tum Scriptorum quorum opera maxime utimur, tum concionatorum pars longe maior, doctrinam hanc proferunt? Nequaquam. Ne γρὺ
An odd conflation of Latin and Greek; the typical Greek form would be μηδὲ γρῦ (‘not even a grunt’); cf. Liddell and Scott, Greek-English Lexicon. quidem de ea ex illis audimus. Ex reliquis autem, perpauci simpliciter eam depingunt, et strenue nobis commendant. At permultos, proh dolor! reperimus, qui de sanctimonia Christiana (vel religione ut vulgo dicitur) ita loquuntur, quasi negativum quid tantummodo foret, quasi is demum Christianus esset censendus, qui non alios execratur aut in vanum iurat; qui non mentitur, non furatur, non maechatur, verbo, qui malum, quod aiunt, non facit. Quod si ulterius aliqui progrediantur, nonne et ipsi, ut plurimum religionem saltem ut externam depingunt? Quasi maxima ex parte, si non omnino in eo poneretur, ut quis beneficus sit, et mediis gratiae utatur? Vel si longius adhuc progrediantur, quid adiiciunt tandem? Nempe, ut verus ille quem vocant Christianus, non modo bonum agat, et a malo se abstineat, sed et recta sentiat, ut sit plane orthodoxus. Et haec demum est religio! Hic pedem figunt, nihil ultra hos limites cernunt, praeter
Monstrum, informe, ingens
Cf. Virgil, Aeneid, iii.658: ‘monstrum horrendum, informe, ingens’ (‘a monster awful, shapeless, huge’).
Horribili super aspectu mortalibus instans,
Cf. Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (On the Nature of Things), i.65: ‘threatening mortals from on high with its horrible visage’. Here, as in An Earnest Appeal, §65, MS reads ‘astans’ instead of ‘instans’. See also No. 142, ‘The Wisdom of Winning Souls’, II, where Wesley says, ‘They apprehend religion as “a terrible spectre looking down from heaven only to enslave the earth, standing over them with so horrible an aspect”.’
cui nomen datur enthusiasmus!
10. Minime tamen me ita accipi velim, quasi vel rectas de rebus divinis opiniones, vel bonum vitae tenorem, vel media illa gratiae, [04:414]despectui habenda censeam. Id longe absit a me. Verum haec omnia quid valent, ab interna religione seiuncta? Quid in ista die nos iuvabunt? Quum venerit Filius hominis cum gloria sua, et sedebit in throno gloriae suae, et cogentur coram eo omnes gentes: num proderit dicere, ‘Domine, non ut reliqui homines fui, rapaces, iniusti, moechi’?
Cf. Luke 18:11 (Beza); see also the quite different Vulgate text: ‘raptores, iniusti, adulteri…’. Non mendax fui, vinolentus, non haereticus? Imo, quid proderit, si non solum a malo nos abstinuimus, sed et alendis egenis omnia insumpsimus, charitatem autem non habeamus?
See 1 Cor. 13:3. Quo tunc animo istos aspiciemus, qui nobis olim toties dixerunt, ‘Dormite quod superest et requiescite’,
Mark 14:41 (Tremellius and Beza). etsi amor Patris non esset in nobis! Qui iustificationem ex operibus quaerere nos docentes, a fide illa gratis accipienda proterruerunt per quam solam verus Dei amor in cordibus nostris potuit effundi!
See Rom. 5:5.
II. Corruptae horum doctrinae maxima ex parte debetur, miseranda nostra quoad mores corruptio; eo iam progressa (ne indicetis in Gath, ne annuntietis in plateis Ashkelon)
Cf. 2 Sam. 1:20 (Tremellius). ut in plerisque neque formam quidem pietatis, nedum potentiam sit invenire.
See 2 Tim. 3:5.
1. Non cum gaudio, sed tristitia cordis loquor, ipsa forma pietatis ubinam est conspicienda? In id vocati sumus omnes, ut simus sancti.
See Rom. 1:7. Quis autem vel speciem sancti prae se fert? Quemvis obvium deprehende, ecce illum alterum! Tertium, quin ad vicesimum si procedas, ne in uno quidem ex iis omnibus vel speciem sancti, magis quam angeli, reperies. Faciem vide, aspectum, corporis gestum. An Deum spirant? An templum Spiritus Sancti indicant? Quin eundem non vice simplici solum, sed et iterum, iterumque observa. Ex aliquo indicio externo posses coniicere, huius in corde Deum habitare? Undenam, quaeso, iudicares, sanguinem Dei pro illius animam fuisse effusum? Haeccine signa immortalis spiritus ad Patrem spirituum proficiscentis?
2. Dices forsan, quid prodest pietatis forma? Nihil sane, si adsit sola. Quod si absit, abest etiam pietatis potentia. Etenim licet illa
sine hac consistere queat, fieri tamen non potest, ut sine pietatis forma, ipsa pietas consistat.
See 2 Tim. 3:5. Externam religionem, ut supra diximus, absque interna saepius videre est. Ubicunque vero deest externa, certo certius est, neque internam posse commorari.
3. Regeret aliquis, ‘Nos vero externam saltem habemus, quippe qui preces publicas ubique locorum celebramus, quibus omnes cuiusvis collegii scholares, tam mane quam vesperi inter esse tenentur.’ Vera dicis, et optandum sane foret, omnes cuiusvis coll[egii] alumnos, seniores praesertim exemplo suo ostensuros, eximium illud privilegium quanti faciant. Num vero omnes qui eisdem intersunt, vel speciem sanctitatis habent? Antequam incipiant sacra, num praesentium vultus ostendit, eos scire, cuius in conspectu se sistunt? Quum peracta fuerint, quonam indicio apparet, aliquid divinum eorum mentibus insedisse? Quin ipso quo peraguntur tempore, ex plurimorum aspectu gestuve quid minus crederes quam illos mentis oculos in Deum defixos habere, quem in medio astantem
See Luke 24:36. certo norunt? Pones ethnicum hominem, linguae nostrae ignarum, in eiusmodi coetum offendere, nullus vereor suspicaretur, nos nunc in eo versari, ut intima animorum sensa coram coeli terraeque Conditore, ac Gubernatore pauperis et egeni proferamus.
4. Num perfectiorem pietatis speciem die Dominica cernimus? Conciones utique publice habentur. Quomodo vero sanctificatur, reliqua diei pars? Num meminimus a quo dictum fuerit, ‘Non facies omne opus in ea: tu, et servus tuus…et advena qui est intra portas tuas’?
Cf. Exod. 20:10 (Vulgate). Quodsi opera quotidiana et ipsi non facimus, et alios, quantum in nobis est, quo minus faciant, prohibemus, nonne sermones caedendo tempus terimus neque nobismet, neque cuilibet alio proficuos? Nonne mere nugationibus totat horas impendimus? Multa agendo, agentes nihil? Sin res ita se habeat, ut os nobis obstruatur necesse est, ipsa specie sanctitatis destitutis.
